---
title: "Does a protective skin microbiome save the population?"
subtitle: "Building the model one piece of biology at a time"
engine: julia
---

## The question

Amphibians can be treated with skin bacteria that inhibit the chytrid fungi *Batrachochytrium
dendrobatidis* (Bd) and *B. salamandrivorans* (Bsal). Would that protect a population?

This vignette answers the question several times over. It starts from the simplest possible
description of treatment and adds one piece of biology at each step. After every step it asks
the same question again, so that the effect of each added piece of realism can be seen.

Two systems are followed in parallel, and a third is used for the final step:

- **Bsal in fire salamanders**, starting from the model of Schmidt et al. (2017);
- **Bd in common toads**, starting from the model of Mitchell et al. (2008);
- **Bd in frogs**, starting from the load model of Briggs et al. (2010), in Part C.

::: {.callout-important}
The two starting models are published and are reproduced here from their papers. Everything
added to them is new work in this package and **is not a published result**. Values taken from
experiments are read from the package's parameter compendium and are named where they are
used. All other added values (efficacy, coverage, spread, exposure windows) are illustrative:
they show what the model does, not what a real treatment would achieve.
:::

```{julia}
using Chytridiomycosis, Plots, Printf
default(linewidth = 2, size = (720, 380), legendfontsize = 8, guidefontsize = 9,
    titlefontsize = 10, left_margin = 4Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 4Plots.mm)

T(; kw...) = MicrobiomeTreatment(; kw...)

# One row per step, filled in as we go and shown as a table at the end.
ladder = NamedTuple[]
step!(system, n, added, outcome, note) = push!(ladder, (; system, n, added, outcome, note))

function ladder_plot(system, xlabel)
    rows = filter(r -> r.system == system, ladder)
    labels = ["$(r.n). $(r.added)" for r in rows]
    bar([r.outcome for r in rows]; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:length(rows), labels),
        yflip = true, legend = false, xlabel, xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1,
        size = (820, 70 + 34 * length(rows)), left_margin = 6Plots.mm, color = :steelblue)
end
```

## Part A. Bsal in fire salamanders

The outcome throughout Part A is the **mean number of adults over the ten years after Bsal
arrives, as a fraction of carrying capacity**. A value of 1 means the population was
untouched.

### Step 0. The host and the pathogen

Schmidt et al. (2017) describe adult female salamanders as susceptible, latent or infectious.
Infectious animals die within about a week.

```{julia}
p = SchmidtParameters(:schmidt2017)
@printf("R0 = %.1f\n", basic_reproduction_number(p))

sli(tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticSLIProblem(p, tr; kw...))
a0 = sli(T())
step!("Bsal", 0, "no treatment", a0.mean_hosts, "population collapses within a year")
plot(a0.t, a0.hosts ./ p.K; xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)",
    label = "no treatment", xlims = (0, 3))
```

With a reproduction number near 25 the population collapses.

### Step 1. A treated class

The simplest description of treatment: an animal is either treated or not, and a treated
animal is infected less often. Every adult is treated once, on the day Bsal arrives, with a
treatment that blocks 99% of infections and lasts for life.

```{julia}
block = T(efficacy = 0.99)
@printf("coverage needed to stop Bsal invading: %.2f\n", critical_coverage(p, block))
a1 = sli(block; coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", 1, "treated class: blocks 99% of infection, for life", a1.mean_hosts,
    "treated adults are safe; their offspring are not")
plot(a1.t, [a1.hosts a1.treated] ./ p.K; label = ["all adults" "treated adults"],
    xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "fraction of K")
```

The treated adults survive, but the population still declines. Recruits are born untreated
and Bsal is still circulating, so each generation of treated animals is replaced by
unprotected ones.

### Step 2. Protection is lost

Applied bacteria do not stay for life. Here a treated animal reverts to untreated with a
half-life of one year.

```{julia}
a2 = sli(T(efficacy = 0.99, half_life = 1.0); coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", 2, "+ protection lost, half-life 1 year", a2.mean_hosts, "collapse is only delayed")
a2.mean_hosts
```

### Step 3. The microbiome spreads between animals

If treated animals pass the bacteria to others, protection can reach the recruits. The
microbiome then has its own reproduction number: the number of animals one treated animal
passes it to before losing it.

```{julia}
spread = T(efficacy = 0.99, half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0)
@printf("microbiome reproduction number %.0f, long-run coverage %.2f\n",
    microbiome_reproduction_number(spread; turnover = p.b), equilibrium_coverage(spread; turnover = p.b))
a3 = sli(spread; coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", 3, "+ microbiome spreads between animals", a3.mean_hosts,
    "full protection: the microbiome maintains itself")
plot(a0.t, a0.hosts ./ p.K; label = "0. no treatment", xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived",
    ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)", legend = :right)
plot!(a1.t, a1.hosts ./ p.K; label = "1. treated class, for life")
plot!(a2.t, a2.hosts ./ p.K; label = "2. + lost with half-life 1 yr")
plot!(a3.t, a3.hosts ./ p.K; label = "3. + spreads between animals")
```

At this level of realism the conclusion would be: **a self-spreading, strongly protective
microbiome works, and nothing else does.**

### Step 4. What trials actually show: survival, not fewer infections

In challenge trials, treated animals were infected as often as untreated ones, but fewer
died. In one trial of *Rana muscosa*, the compendium records these counts:

```{julia}
h = parameter_set(:harris2009ismej)
mortality_reduction(h.deaths_treated, h.n_treated, h.deaths_control, h.n_control)
```

So the treated class is changed: instead of blocking infection, treatment reduces
disease-induced death (`tolerance`). A treated, infected animal stays infectious.

```{julia}
tolerant = T(tolerance = 0.9, half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0)
@printf("Bsal reproduction number if everyone is treated: %.0f (untreated %.0f)\n",
    effective_reproduction_number(p, tolerant, 1.0), basic_reproduction_number(p))
a4 = sli(tolerant; coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", 4, "+ protection as in trials: survive, still infected", a4.mean_hosts,
    "fails, and raises transmission: survivors shed for longer")
a4.mean_hosts
```

The same spreading microbiome now fails. Animals that survive infection shed for longer, so
Bsal's reproduction number goes up, not down.

### Step 5. Lower pathogen load: less death and less shedding

A microbiome that suppresses the fungus should lower the load on the animal. Lower load means
less shedding as well as less death. Here both follow from one reduction in load: shedding in
proportion to load, death in proportion to load raised to a power `k`.

```{julia}
reductions = [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999]
ks = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0]
R = [effective_reproduction_number(p, load_reducing_treatment(ρ; death_exponent = k), 1.0)
     for ρ in reductions, k in ks]
plot(string.(reductions), R; yscale = :log10, marker = :circle, xlabel = "reduction in load",
    ylabel = "Bsal reproduction number, all treated",
    label = permutedims(["k = $k" for k in ks]), legend = :topright)
hline!([1.0]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "threshold")
```

With death proportional to load (`k = 1`) the two effects nearly cancel: the animal sheds less
but for longer. Only a very large reduction brings the reproduction number below 1.

```{julia}
a5 = sli(load_reducing_treatment(0.99; half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0); coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", 5, "+ lower load (99%): less death and less shedding", a5.mean_hosts,
    "partial; survivors remain infected")
(mean_adults = a5.mean_hosts, final_prevalence = a5.final_prevalence)
```

### Step 6. Larvae

Schmidt's model has adults only. Fire salamander larvae can be infected experimentally
without showing disease, and half of them carried the infection through metamorphosis (Wang
et al. 2021; the count is read from the compendium).

```{julia}
stage = BsalLarvalStage(:wang2021; adult_to_larva = 5.2)
@printf("carry-over through metamorphosis: %.1f\n", stage.carry_over)
b0 = solve(BsalLarvalProblem(p, stage))
plot(a0.t, max.(a0.hosts ./ p.K, 1e-12); yscale = :log10, label = "adults only (step 0)",
    xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)", legend = :bottomright)
plot!(b0.t, b0.adults ./ p.K; label = "with a larval stage")
```

Adding the stage changes the untreated outcome. Larvae already in the water metamorphose after
the adult epidemic has burnt out, so the population no longer falls to vanishingly small
numbers. The near-extinction in the adults-only model was partly a result of having no other
stage.

Treatment is now put on this model, going back to the infection-blocking treatment of step 1
so that the effect of the stage itself is clear.

```{julia}
lar(tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticLarvalProblem(p, stage, tr; coverage = 1.0, kw...))
a6 = lar(block)
step!("Bsal", 6, "+ larval stage (treatment as in step 1)", a6.mean_adults,
    "as step 1: recruits still unprotected")
a6.mean_adults
```

### Step 7. Treat the right stage

With larvae in the model, treatment can be given to them too. Two new unknowns link the
stages: whether a treated larva keeps the bacteria through metamorphosis (`retention`), and
whether a treated mother's larvae are born with them (`maternal`).

```{julia}
quarterly = 0:0.25:9.75
strategies = [
    ("adults, once", (;)),
    ("larvae, quarterly; lost at metamorphosis", (treat = :larvae, treat_times = quarterly)),
    ("larvae, quarterly; kept", (treat = :larvae, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)),
    ("both stages, quarterly; kept", (treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)),
]
vals = [lar(block; kw...).mean_adults for (_, kw) in strategies]
bar(vals; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:4, first.(strategies)), yflip = true, legend = false,
    xlabel = "mean adults (fraction of K)", xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1,
    left_margin = 6Plots.mm, size = (820, 230), color = :steelblue)
```

```{julia}
a7 = lar(block; treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", 7, "+ treat both stages, kept through metamorphosis", a7.mean_adults,
    "full protection with no spread at all")
a7.mean_adults
```

This overturns the conclusion of step 3. Once recruits can be treated before they become
adults, **the microbiome does not need to spread**. It does need to survive metamorphosis,
and that has not been measured.

### Step 8. How long the bacteria really last

Two open datasets (a field trial in *Rana sierrae* and a laboratory trial in *Xenopus laevis*)
give the abundance of applied bacteria over time. Fitting an exponential decline to them gives
half-lives of 3 to 14 days; in the field, 4 to 5 days. (The fits are this project's own and
are described in the project wiki.)

Protection now wanes with abundance. `protective_fold` is how far abundance can fall before
half the effect is lost; nobody has measured it, so three values are shown.

```{julia}
days = 0:1:150
plot(xlabel = "days since application", ylabel = "fraction of full protection", legend = :topright)
for F in (10.0, 100.0, 1000.0)
    w = T(efficacy = 0.99, abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = F)
    plot!(days, [protection(w, d / 365) for d in days];
        label = @sprintf("fold %g: half gone after %.0f days", F, 365 * protection_duration(w)))
end
current()
```

```{julia}
waning = T(efficacy = 0.99, abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = 100.0)
a8 = lar(waning; treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", 8, "+ measured decay (half-life 5 days), dosed quarterly", a8.mean_adults,
    "fails: protection lasts about a month; monthly dosing reaches 0.28")
monthly = lar(waning; treat = :both, treat_times = 0:(1 / 12):9.95, retention = 1.0)
(quarterly = a8.mean_adults, monthly = monthly.mean_adults)
```

### Part A summary

```{julia}
ladder_plot("Bsal", "mean adults over 10 years, fraction of K")
```

## Part B. Bd in common toads

The outcome throughout Part B is the **number of adults over the last ten of 35 years, as a
fraction of the number without Bd**, together with whether Bd persists. The parameter set is
the one behind Figure 2d of Mitchell et al. (2008), in which Bd drives the toads extinct and
then dies out itself.

### Step 0. The host and the pathogen

In Mitchell's model only tadpoles are infected. Infected tadpoles are removed at
metamorphosis, and zoospores live in the pond.

```{julia}
m = MitchellParameters(:mitchell2008; set = "fig2d")
pond(tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticPondProblem(m, tr; kw...))
rel(r) = r.A_mean / r.A_disease_free
show_pond(r) = (adults = round(rel(r), digits = 2), toads_persist = r.toads_persist, bd_persists = r.bd_persist)

b0 = pond(T())
step!("Bd toad", 0, "no treatment", rel(b0), "toads and Bd both go extinct")
show_pond(b0)
```

### Step 1. A treated class

Each year 80% of tadpoles are treated at hatching with a treatment that blocks 90% of
infections and lasts the season.

```{julia}
b1 = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9); coverage = 0.8)
step!("Bd toad", 1, "treated class: 80% of tadpoles, blocks 90%", rel(b1), "toads saved, Bd eliminated")
adults(r) = (r.t[r.t .>= -2], r.A[r.t .>= -2] ./ r.A_disease_free)
plot(adults(b0)...; label = "0. no treatment", xlabel = "years since Bd arrived",
    ylabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", legend = :right)
plot!(adults(b1)...; label = "1. tadpoles treated every year")
```

Unlike Bsal, the simplest treatment works here. The infected stage is short and a new cohort
can be treated every year. It does not prevent the initial crash: adults fall to a few percent
of their former number before Bd dies out and the population recovers over two decades.

### Step 2. Protection is lost

```{julia}
b2 = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9, half_life = 0.05); coverage = 0.8)
step!("Bd toad", 2, "+ protection lost, half-life 18 days", rel(b2), "still works: the season is short")
show_pond(b2)
```

### Step 3. Stop treating and rely on spread

Can treatment stop after five years if the bacteria persist in the pond and reach new
tadpoles from there?

```{julia}
b3 = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9, environmental = 50.0, reservoir_half_life = 1.0); coverage = 0.8,
    treat_years = 0:4)
step!("Bd toad", 3, "+ treat 5 years only, bacteria persist in pond", rel(b3),
    "fails once treatment stops")
show_pond(b3)
```

The field trial behind step 8 found that the applied bacterium spread to untreated frogs
within days but then declined everywhere, so this step is not rescued by the evidence either.
The remaining steps go back to treating every year.

### Step 4. Survival, not fewer infections

As in Part A, treatment now lets infected tadpoles live instead of preventing infection.

```{julia}
b4 = pond(T(tolerance = 0.7); coverage = 0.8)
step!("Bd toad", 4, "+ protection as in trials: survive, still infected", rel(b4),
    "toads persist at lower numbers; Bd is no longer eliminated")
show_pond(b4)
```

The toads are saved, but Bd now stays in the pond for good, so treatment can never stop.

### Step 5. Lower load

```{julia}
b5 = pond(load_reducing_treatment(0.7); coverage = 0.8)
step!("Bd toad", 5, "+ lower load (70%): less death and less shedding", rel(b5),
    "little changed: untreated tadpoles and the pond keep Bd going")
show_pond(b5)
```

### Step 6. Infection after metamorphosis

Mitchell's model removes every infected tadpole at metamorphosis. Experiments show that
toadlets exposed to Bd are infected, that most die, and that some survive (Smith et al. 2022;
counts from the compendium).

```{julia}
s = parameter_set(:smith2022)
survival = 1 - s.deaths_exposed / s.n_exposed
stages = PostMetamorphicInfection(metamorph_survival = survival)
@printf("toadlet survival after exposure: %.2f\n", survival)
c0 = pond(T(); stages)
show_pond(c0)
```

This changes the untreated outcome: with some infected metamorphs surviving, the toads no
longer go extinct, and so neither does Bd. The published "both die out" result depended on
every infected animal dying.

```{julia}
effs = [0.5, 0.9, 0.99]
tols = [0.3, 0.7, 1.0]
blocking = [rel(pond(T(efficacy = e); coverage = 0.8, stages)) for e in effs]
tolerating = [rel(pond(T(tolerance = τ); coverage = 0.8, stages)) for τ in tols]
plot(["0.5", "0.9", "0.99"], blocking; marker = :circle, label = "blocks infection (efficacy)",
    xlabel = "strength of treatment", ylabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", ylims = (0, 1),
    legend = :topleft)
plot!(["0.5", "0.9", "0.99"], tolerating; marker = :square,
    label = "survives infection (tolerance 0.3, 0.7, 1.0)")
```

```{julia}
b6 = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9); coverage = 0.8, stages)
step!("Bd toad", 6, "+ infected metamorphs can survive (treatment as in step 1)", rel(b6),
    "blocking infection no longer eliminates Bd or protects well")
b6t = pond(T(tolerance = 0.7); coverage = 0.8, stages)
step!("Bd toad", 7, "same, with survival-type protection", rel(b6t),
    "now the better mechanism: the ranking has reversed")
(blocking = show_pond(b6), tolerating = show_pond(b6t))
```

In step 1, blocking infection eliminated Bd. With the more realistic life cycle it does not,
and the treatment that lets animals survive infection now does better. **Which mechanism is
best depends on a detail of the host's life cycle, not on the treatment.**

### Step 8. How long the bacteria really last

With the measured decay, one dose at hatching wanes during the 95-day tadpole season. More
doses in the season restore much of it.

```{julia}
waning_t = T(tolerance = 0.7, abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = 100.0)
schedules = [("at hatching only", Float64[]), ("+ day 45", [45.0]), ("+ days 30, 60", [30.0, 60.0]),
    ("+ days 20, 40, 60, 80", [20.0, 40.0, 60.0, 80.0])]
doses = [rel(pond(waning_t; coverage = 0.8, stages, redose_days = d)) for (_, d) in schedules]
bar(doses; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:4, first.(schedules)), yflip = true, legend = false,
    xlabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1,
    left_margin = 6Plots.mm, size = (820, 230), color = :steelblue)
```

```{julia}
step!("Bd toad", 8, "+ measured decay, one dose at hatching", doses[1], "protection gone before the season ends")
step!("Bd toad", 9, "+ three doses per season", doses[3], "about two-thirds of the benefit restored; five doses do better")
doses
```

### Part B summary

```{julia}
ladder_plot("Bd toad", "adults in years 25 to 35, fraction of disease-free")
```

## Part C. Bd in frogs: bacteria as a state of each animal

Parts A and B gave every treated animal the same clock. The last step removes that
simplification, in a third system where it is natural to do so: frogs sharing a pool, with
disease driven by the fungal load on each frog (after Briggs et al. 2010, with the saturating
clearance added in this package's load tipping model). Here 80 frogs share a pool, which is
enough for loads to run away, and untreated they all die.

Each frog now carries its own abundance of the applied bacteria. Abundance declines at the
measured rate, and frogs exchange bacteria through the pond. Exchange moves bacteria between
frogs without creating any, so the bacteria spread but do not sustain themselves. That is what
the field trial showed: eleven days after 60 to 90% of the frogs in a pond were bathed, frogs
that were never bathed carried about 0.63 times as much of the bacterium as bathed ones, and
it then declined in both.

```{julia}
pb = BriggsParameters(:briggs2010)
frog = (c = 100.0, c_treated = 300.0, h = 500.0, N = 80, ε = 1000.0)
baths(; x = 0.1, F = 100.0, coverage = 0.75, dose_days = [0], days = 730) =
    solve(ProbioticAbundanceProblem(pb, T(abundance_half_life = 5.0, protective_fold = F, direct = x);
        frog..., coverage, dose_days, days))

for x in (0.0, 0.1, 1.0)
    r = baths(; x, days = 30)
    @printf("exchange %.1f per day: unbathed/bathed abundance on day 11 = %.2f\n", x,
        r.abundance_unbathed[12] / r.abundance_bathed[12])
end
```

An exchange rate of about 0.1 per day reproduces the field ratio, and is used below.

```{julia}
untreated = baths(coverage = 0.0)
one = baths()
every90 = baths(dose_days = 0:90:729)
plot(untreated.t, max.(untreated.mean_load, 1.0); yscale = :log10, label = "no treatment",
    xlabel = "days", ylabel = "mean Bd load per live frog", legend = :topright, xlims = (0, 730))
plot!(one.t, max.(one.mean_load, 1.0); label = "one bath on day 0")
plot!(every90.t, max.(every90.mean_load, 1.0); label = "a bath every 90 days")
hline!([pb.Smax]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "lethal load")
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
first_death(r) = any(>(0), r.death_day) ? minimum(filter(>(0), r.death_day)) : 0
println("| Baths | Alive after 2 years (of 80) | First death (day) |")
println("|---|---|---|")
for (label, r) in (("none", untreated), ("one, day 0", one), ("every 240 days", baths(dose_days = 0:240:729)),
        ("every 150 days", baths(dose_days = 0:150:729)), ("every 90 days", every90),
        ("every 90 days, 10% of frogs", baths(coverage = 0.1, dose_days = 0:90:729)),
        ("every 90 days, 10% of frogs, no exchange", baths(coverage = 0.1, x = 0.0, dose_days = 0:90:729)),
        ("one, day 150 (loads already high)", baths(dose_days = [150])))
    @printf("| %s | %d | %s |\n", label, r.alive[end], first_death(r) == 0 ? "none" : string(first_death(r)))
end
```

```{julia}
step!("Bd frog", 0, "no treatment", untreated.alive[end] / 80, "all die at about day 156")
step!("Bd frog", 1, "bacteria on each frog, measured decay: one bath", one.alive[end] / 80,
    "die-off delayed by about six weeks")
step!("Bd frog", 2, "+ a bath every 90 days", every90.alive[end] / 80,
    "all survive: each bath resets the slow build-up of load")
```

This is the one system where bacteria that last only weeks could still work. Disease here
depends on load, and load takes months to build. A short burst of extra clearance knocks it
back, and the build-up starts again. Because frogs exchange bacteria, bathing a small part of
the population protects the rest.

Two cautions. The slow build-up is for a population that starts clean. In the field trial the
pond was in the middle of an outbreak, treated frogs were surrounded by heavily infected ones,
and their loads were back within two months; the last row of the table is the model's version
of treating too late. And the size of the clearance effect of the bacteria is assumed, not
measured.

## What each piece of realism did

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("| System | Step | Added | Outcome | What changed |")
println("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for r in ladder
    @printf("| %s | %d | %s | %.2f | %s |\n", r.system, r.n, r.added, r.outcome, r.note)
end
```

Reading down the table:

1. **The answer changed at almost every step**, and it changed direction more than once. A
   model stopped at step 3 says a self-spreading microbiome is essential for Bsal. Stopped at
   step 7 it says spread is unnecessary. Stopped at step 8 it says neither is achievable with
   bacteria that last a few weeks.
2. **How protection works matters more than how strong it is.** Blocking infection and
   surviving infection give opposite population-level results for Bsal, and swap rank in
   toads when the life cycle is made more realistic.
3. **Life-cycle detail in the host model changed the conclusions as much as anything in the
   treatment model.** Larvae in the Bsal model, and surviving metamorphs in the toad model,
   each overturned a result.
4. **The systems differ for structural reasons.** A toad cohort passes through a short
   infected stage once a year and can be re-treated. A salamander must be protected for
   life against a pathogen that kills in a week. In frogs, where disease follows a load that
   builds slowly, short-lived bacteria can still work if they are re-applied.

## What is not in the model

- In Parts A and B bacterial abundance is a clock since the last dose, not a state of each
  animal. Only the frog model of Part C tracks it per animal.
- The fold-drop in abundance at which protection is lost has not been measured.
- Whether applied bacteria survive metamorphosis has not been measured.
- The Bsal model has no recovery from infection and no years between metamorphosis and
  maturity. The toad model has thresholds standing in for extinction, and adult toads that
  carry Bd are not yet combined with treatment.
- Everything is deterministic.

## References
